title: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz
hook: a caliph of the ruling family who began his reforms with his own family's wealth

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arabic coins and offices: Arabic became the language of the government's records, and coins carried verses where a ruler's face might have been. Your line was: words instead of faces. Did you read the writing on a coin? Day nine hundred seven.

A lamp is burning on a desk in Damascus. A visitor comes in, and once the state's business is done, the talk turns to family news. The man at the desk reaches over, puts the lamp out, and lights a different one. The first lamp, he explains, burns oil paid for by the public treasury. This conversation is his own, so it gets his own lamp. That is a story people tell about Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, an Umayyad caliph. Whether or not it happened just that way, it shows what people remembered about him: a ruler who kept careful track of what was his and what belonged to everyone. Today: the caliph they called just.
screen: `A LAMP ON A DESK.` → `PUT OUT FOR A PRIVATE TALK.` → `WHAT IS MINE, WHAT IS EVERYONE'S.`

segments.voice: Start with the girl and the milk, another story people tell. The caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab is walking Medina by night. Through a wall he hears a mother tell her daughter to stretch the milk with water before selling it. The daughter says the caliph has forbidden that. The mother says the caliph can't see them. And the girl answers: if Umar does not see, the Lord of Umar sees. The story says Umar married her to his son. Her daughter's son was Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz. So he is the just grandson: the girl who would not cheat in the dark was his grandmother, and the caliph who heard her was his forebear. Now the man himself. He was born into the ruling family and raised in comfort, and the histories say he was a governor of Medina before he became caliph. When he took power, the reports say he started with his own house. Lands and goods that his family had taken unjustly, he returned, beginning with what he held himself. His wife Fatima, a caliph's daughter, is reported to have given her jewels to the treasury. He also ended something ugly. Under earlier Umayyad rulers, Ali ibn Abi Talib had been cursed from the pulpits. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz stopped it, and the reports say the Friday sermon came to close with a verse instead, the one that begins, in Pickthall's translation, "Lo! Allah enjoineth justice and kindness." His rule was short. But some Sunni scholars later counted him with the rightly guided caliphs, calling him the fifth. A ruler remembered not for what he took, but for what he gave back.
screen: `THE GIRL AND THE MILK.` · `HE STARTED WITH HIS OWN HOUSE.` · `THE CURSING STOPPED.` · then, large: `JUSTICE AND KINDNESS.`

segments.voice: The practice: live simply for a day. Sit comfortably and let your breathing slow. Bring to mind the two lamps on the desk. Breathe in. Name one thing in your life that is more than you need: a subscription, a second helping, an extra hour on a screen. Breathe out. Hold it lightly and ask whether you need it or only want it. Then choose one comfort to go without today, something small enough that you'll really do it. If you pray, you can ask for contentment in your own words. If you don't, just rest with the question of what is enough. The bell holds the time.
Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz. An Umayyad caliph remembered for justice and simple living, who returned what his own family had taken and ended the cursing from the pulpits. Today's word.
Your line: the just grandson. Today, live simply: give up one small comfort, and notice what fills the space it leaves. Day nine hundred seven.

howItsDone: Muslims often tell stories of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, such as the two lamps, when they talk about honest leadership and keeping public money apart from private use.

original.note: Arabic: Umar, son of Abd al-Aziz. Abd al-Aziz means servant of the Mighty, one of the names of God.

what a scholar hears: some Sunni scholars counted him among the rightly guided caliphs, and his descent through his mother is traced to Umar ibn al-Khattab.
